{{MOS|article|date=July 2025| [[MOS:FORMULA]] - avoid mixing {{tag|math}} and {{tl|math}} in the same expression}}
In mathematics, the '''Kontsevich quantization formula''' describes how to construct a generalized [[Moyal product|★-product]] [[operator algebra]] from a given arbitrary finite-dimensional [[Poisson manifold]]. This operator algebra amounts to the [[deformation quantization]] of the corresponding Poisson algebra. It is due to [[Maxim Kontsevich]].<ref>M. Kontsevich (2003), [https://arxiv.org/abs/q-alg/9709040 ''Deformation Quantization of Poisson Manifolds''], ''Letters of Mathematical Physics'' '''66''', pp. 157&ndash;216.</ref><ref>{{cite journal |author1=[[Alberto Cattaneo|Cattaneo, Alberto]] |author2=[[Giovanni Felder|Felder, Giovanni]] | year = 2000 | title = A Path Integral Approach to the Kontsevich Quantization Formula | journal = Communications in Mathematical Physics | volume = 212 | issue = 3 | pages = 591–611 | doi = 10.1007/s002200000229| arxiv = math/9902090| bibcode = 2000CMaPh.212..591C| s2cid = 8510811 }}</ref>

==Deformation quantization of a Poisson algebra==
Given a [[Poisson algebra]] {{math|(''A'', {⋅, ⋅})}}, a [[Deformation theory|deformation]] quantization is an '''associative''' unital product  <math>\star</math> on the algebra of formal [[power series]] in {{math|''ħ'', ''A''<nowiki>[[</nowiki>''ħ''<nowiki>]]</nowiki>}}, subject to the following two axioms,

:<math>\begin{align}
 f\star g &=fg+\mathcal{O}(\hbar)\\
{}[f,g] &=f\star g-g\star f=i\hbar\{f,g\}+\mathcal{O}(\hbar^2)
\end{align}</math>

If one were given a Poisson manifold {{math|(''M'', {⋅, ⋅})}}, one could ask, in addition, that

:<math>f\star g=fg+\sum_{k=1}^\infty \hbar^kB_k(f\otimes g),</math>

where the {{mvar|B<sub>k</sub>}} are linear bi[[differential operator]]s of degree at most {{mvar|k}}.

Two deformations are said to be equivalent iff they are related by a gauge transformation of the type,
:<math>\begin{cases}
D: A[[\hbar]]\to A[[\hbar]] \\ 
\sum_{k=0}^\infty \hbar^k f_k \mapsto \sum_{k=0}^\infty \hbar^k f_k +\sum_{n\ge1, k\ge0} D_n(f_k)\hbar^{n+k}
\end{cases}</math>
where {{mvar|D<sub>n</sub>}} are differential operators of order at most {{mvar|n}}. The corresponding induced <math>\star</math>-product, <math>\star'</math>, is then 
:<math>f\,{\star}'\,g = D \left ( \left (D^{-1}f \right )\star \left (D^{-1}g \right ) \right ).</math>

For the archetypal example, one may well consider [[Hilbrand J. Groenewold|Groenewold]]'s original [[Wigner–Weyl transform|"Moyal&ndash;Weyl" <math>\star</math>-product]].

==Kontsevich graphs==
A Kontsevich graph is a simple [[directed graph]] without loops on 2 external vertices, labeled ''f'' and ''g''; and {{mvar|n}} internal vertices, labeled {{math|Π}}. From each internal vertex originate two edges. All (equivalence classes of) graphs with {{mvar|n}} internal vertices are accumulated in the set {{math|''G<sub>n</sub>''(2)}}.

An example on two internal vertices is the following graph,
:[[Image:KontsevichGraph2.svg|Kontsevich graph for n=2]]

===Associated bidifferential operator===
Associated to each graph {{math|Γ}}, there is a bidifferential operator {{math|''B''<sub>Γ</sub>( ''f'', ''g'')}} defined as follows.  For each edge there is a [[partial derivative]] on the symbol of the target vertex. It is contracted with the corresponding index from the source symbol. The term for the graph {{math|Γ}} is the product of all its symbols together with their partial derivatives. Here ''f'' and ''g'' stand for smooth functions on the manifold, and {{math|Π}} is the [[Poisson bivector]] of the Poisson manifold.

The term for the example graph is

:<math>\Pi^{i_2j_2}\partial_{i_2}\Pi^{i_1j_1}\partial_{i_1}f\,\partial_{j_1}\partial_{j_2}g.</math>

===Associated weight===
For adding up these bidifferential operators there are the weights {{math|''w''<sub>Γ</sub>}} of the graph {{math|Γ}}. First of all, to each graph there is a multiplicity {{math|''m''(Γ)}} which counts how many equivalent configurations there are for one graph. The rule is that the sum of the multiplicities for all graphs with {{mvar|n}} internal vertices is {{math|(''n''(''n'' + 1))<sup>''n''</sup>}}. The sample graph above has the multiplicity {{math|''m''(Γ) {{=}} 8}}. For this, it is helpful to enumerate the internal vertices from 1 to {{mvar|n}}.

In order to compute the weight we have to integrate products of the angle in the [[upper half-plane]], ''H'', as follows. The upper half-plane is {{math|''H'' ⊂ <math>\mathbb{C}</math>}}, endowed with the [[Poincaré metric]]

:<math>ds^2=\frac{dx^2+dy^2}{y^2};</math>

and, for two points {{math|''z'', ''w'' ∈ ''H''}} with {{math|''z'' ≠ ''w''}}, we measure the angle {{mvar|φ}} between the geodesic from {{mvar|z}} to {{math|''i''∞}} and from {{mvar|z}} to {{mvar|w}} counterclockwise. This is

:<math>\phi(z,w)=\frac{1}{2i}\log\frac{(z-w)(z-\bar{w})}{(\bar{z}-w)(\bar{z}-\bar{w})}.</math>

The integration domain is ''C''<sub>''n''</sub>(''H'') the space
:<math>C_n(H):=\{(u_1,\dots,u_n)\in H^n: u_i\ne u_j\forall i\ne j\}.</math>

The formula amounts
:<math>w_\Gamma:= \frac{m(\Gamma)}{(2\pi)^{2n}n!}\int_{C_n(H)} \bigwedge_{j=1}^n\mathrm{d}\phi(u_j,u_{t1(j)})\wedge\mathrm{d}\phi(u_j,u_{t2(j)})</math>,
where ''t''1(''j'') and ''t''2(''j'') are the first and second target vertex of the internal vertex {{mvar|j}}. The vertices ''f'' and ''g'' are at the fixed positions 0 and 1 in {{mvar|H}}.

==The formula==
Given the above three definitions, the Kontsevich formula for a star product is now
:<math>f\star g = fg+\sum_{n=1}^\infty\left(\frac{i\hbar}{2}\right)^n \sum_{\Gamma \in G_n(2)} w_\Gamma B_\Gamma(f\otimes g).</math>

===Explicit formula up to second order===
Enforcing associativity of the <math>\star</math>-product, it is straightforward to check directly that the Kontsevich formula must reduce, to second order in {{mvar|ħ}}, to just

:<math>\begin{align}
f\star g &= fg +\tfrac{i\hbar}{2}\Pi^{ij}\partial_i f\,\partial_j g -\tfrac{\hbar^2}{8}\Pi^{i_1j_1}\Pi^{i_2j_2}\partial_{i_1}\,\partial_{i_2}f \partial_{j_1}\,\partial_{j_2}g\\
& - \tfrac{\hbar^2}{12}\Pi^{i_1j_1}\partial_{j_1}\Pi^{i_2j_2}(\partial_{i_1}\partial_{i_2}f \,\partial_{j_2}g -\partial_{i_2}f\,\partial_{i_1}\partial_{j_2}g) +\mathcal{O}(\hbar^3)
\end{align}</math>
